title: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (runner's knee)
intro: Patellofemoral pain syndrome causes pain around or behind the kneecap, especially when climbing stairs, squatting, running or sitting for long periods with bent knees. It is common in young, active people. It usually improves with exercise therapy and activity adjustment rather than surgery.

sections.heading: Causes
paragraphs: The kneecap glides in a groove at the end of the thigh bone. Irritation may result when the load is too high or the kneecap does not track smoothly. Contributing factors include a sudden increase in running or training, weakness of thigh and hip muscles, tight muscles, flat feet, previous injury and unsuitable footwear. Often several factors combine.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: A dull ache at the front of the knee, aggravated by stairs, hills, squatting, running and prolonged sitting. Some people feel grinding or clicking. Swelling is usually mild, and the knee does not give way or lock, which would suggest other problems.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Doctors diagnose it from the history and examination. Scans are usually not needed unless an injury, swelling or locking suggests something else. Cartilage changes on imaging do not always match pain.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Exercise is the cornerstone. Strengthening the thigh and hip muscles with a programme over at least several weeks reduces pain. Temporarily reduce activities that provoke symptoms and switch to low-impact options such as cycling or swimming, then build up again gradually. Taping or a brace may give short-term relief. Insoles can help some people. Painkillers can be used for short periods.
Surgery is rarely needed. Many people improve within three to six months, though recovery can take longer.

sections.heading: Preventing recurrence
paragraphs: Increase training gradually, choose suitable shoes, warm up, include strength work for hips and thighs and avoid sudden jumps in distance or hill work.

examples.title: Adjusting your training
examples.text: Imagine your knee hurts after a rise in running distance. You could swap some runs for cycling, start strengthening exercises and increase distances slowly once the pain eases.

examples.title: Sitting comfortably
examples.text: Suppose sitting through a long meeting causes pain. You might stand and stretch your legs periodically and avoid keeping the knees tightly bent.
